'''Lean''' is a [[proof assistant]] and a [[Functional programming|functional]] [[programming language]].<ref name="Lean4ProgLang">{{Cite book |last1=Moura |first1=Leonardo de |author1-link=Leonardo de Moura |last2=Ullrich |first2=Sebastian |date=2021 |editor1-last=Platzer |editor1-first=André |editor2-last=Sutcliffe |editor2-first=Geoff |chapter=The Lean 4 Theorem Prover and Programming Language |title=Automated Deduction – CADE 28 |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=12699 |language=en |location=Cham |publisher=Springer International Publishing |pages=625–635 |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37 |isbn=978-3-030-79876-5|doi-access=free}}</ref> It is based on the [[calculus of constructions]] with [[inductive type]]s (specifically, the Calculus of Inductive Constructions), the foundational type theory developed with the [[Rocq|Coq]] theorem prover,<ref>{{cite conference |last1=Paulin-Mohring |first1=Christine |title=Inductive definitions in the system Coq: Rules and properties |book-title=Typed Lambda Calculi and Applications |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |volume=664 |publisher=Springer |year=1993 |pages=328–345 |doi=10.1007/BFb0037116}}</ref> which was renamed to [[Rocq]] in 2024.<ref>{{cite web |title=The Rocq Prover |url=https://rocq-prover.org/ |website=rocq-prover.org |access-date=July 26, 2026}}</ref> It is a [[free and open-source software]] project hosted on [[GitHub]]. Development is currently supported by the [[Nonprofit organization|nonprofit]] Lean [[Convergent Research|Focused Research Organization]] (FRO). 

== History ==
Lean was developed primarily by Brazilian computer scientist [[Leonardo de Moura]] while employed by [[Microsoft Research]] and now [[Amazon Web Services]] and has had significant contributions from other coauthors and collaborators during its history.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Contributors to leanprover/lean4 |url=https://github.com/leanprover/lean4/graphs/contributors?all=1 |access-date=2026-08-11 |website=GitHub}}</ref>

Launched in 2013,<ref>{{Cite web |title=About |url=https://lean-lang.org/about/ |access-date=2024-03-13 |website=Lean Language}}</ref> initial versions of the language, later known as Lean 1 and 2, were experimental and contained features such as support for [[homotopy type theory]]-based foundations that were later dropped.

Lean 3 (first released Jan 20, 2017) was the first moderately stable version of Lean. It was implemented primarily in [[C++]] with some features written in Lean itself. After version 3.4.2, Lean 3 was officially end-of-lifed while development of Lean 4 began. In this interim period members of the Lean community developed and released unofficial versions up to 3.51.1.<ref>{{cite web |title=leanprover-community/lean - Lean 3 Theorem Prover (community fork) |url=https://github.com/leanprover-community/lean |website=GitHub |access-date=2026-07-31}}</ref>

In 2021, Lean 4 was released, which was a reimplementation of the Lean theorem prover capable of producing [[C (programming language)|C]] code which is then compiled, enabling the development of efficient domain-specific automation.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Moura |first1=Leonardo de |last2=Ullrich |first2=Sebastian |editor1-last=Platzer |editor1-first=Andr'e |editor2-last=Sutcliffe |editor2-first=Geoff |title=Automated Deduction -- CADE 28 |date=2021 |publisher=Springer International Publishing |isbn=978-3-030-79876-5 |pages=625–635 |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37 |s2cid=235800962 |url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-79876-5_37 |access-date=24 March 2023}}</ref> Lean 4 also contains a [[hygienic macro]] system and improved [[type class]] synthesis and memory management procedures over the previous version.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ullrich |first1=Sebastian |last2=de Moura |first2=Leonardo |date=2020-01-28 |title=Beyond Notations: Hygienic Macro Expansion for Theorem Proving Languages |journal=Logical Methods in Computer Science |article-number=7421 |doi=10.46298/lmcs-18(2:1)2022 |arxiv=2001.10490 }}</ref> Another benefit compared to Lean 3 is the ability to avoid touching C++ code in order to modify the frontend and other key parts of the core system, as they are now all implemented in Lean and available to the end user to be overridden as needed.<ref name="Lean4ProgLang" />

Lean 4 is not [[Backward compatibility|backwards-compatible]] with Lean 3.<ref>{{cite web |title=Significant changes from Lean 3 |url=https://leanprover.github.io/lean4/doc/lean3changes.html |website=Lean Manual |access-date=24 March 2023 |archive-date=15 March 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230315004639/https://leanprover.github.io/lean4/doc/lean3changes.html |url-status=dead }}</ref> It uses the [[C++17]] version of C++.<ref name="Lean4ProgLang"/>

In 2023, the Lean FRO (Focused Research Organization) was formed, with the goals of improving the language's scalability and usability, and implementing [[proof automation]].<ref>{{Cite web |date=2023-07-25 |title=Mission |url=https://lean-fro.org/about/ |access-date=2024-03-14 |website=Lean FRO}}</ref>

In 2025, [[Association for Computing Machinery|ACM]] [[SIGPLAN#Programming Languages Software Award|SIGPLAN Programming Languages Software Award]] was awarded to Gabriel Ebner, Soonho Kong, [[Leonardo de Moura|Leo de Moura]] and Sebastian Ullrich for Lean, cited for its "significant impact on mathematics, hardware and software verification, and AI".<ref>{{Cite web |title=Programming Languages Software Award |url=https://www.sigplan.org/Awards/Software/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250706180156/https://www.sigplan.org/Awards/Software/ |access-date=2025-07-06 |archive-date=6 Jul 2025 |website=www.sigplan.org}}</ref>

In 2026, the [[#Libraries|''mathlib'' library]] was awarded the Demailly prize for [[open science]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Épijournal de Géométrie Algébrique - 2026 Demailly Prize |url=https://epiga.episciences.org/page/session-2026 |access-date=2026-05-26 |website=epiga.episciences.org |language=fr}}</ref>

== Overview ==

Lean includes many features useful for functional programming and theorem proving, such as [[dependent types]], [[type classes]], multi-threading, an expressive tactic language, and a module system.<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Lean Language Reference |url=https://lean-lang.org/doc/reference/latest/ |access-date=2025-12-25 |website=Lean Language}}</ref>

=== Libraries ===

The official Lean [[standard library]] is called ''Std'' and contains common [[data structure]]s and functions useful for programming, such as tree maps, hash maps, datetime functions, and concurrency primitives.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Std |url=https://lean-lang.org/doc/api/Std.html |access-date=2025-12-25 |website=Lean Language}}</ref> The standard library is complemented by the community-maintained ''batteries'', which implements additional data structures that may be used for both mathematical research and more conventional software development.<ref>{{Cite web |title=batteries |url=https://github.com/leanprover-community/batteries |access-date=2024-09-22 |website=[[GitHub]]}}</ref>

In 2017, a community-maintained project to develop a Lean library ''mathlib'' began, with the goal to digitize as much of [[pure mathematics]] as possible in one large cohesive library, up to research level mathematics.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Building the Mathematical Library of the Future |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/building-the-mathematical-library-of-the-future-20201001/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260329223710/https://www.quantamagazine.org/building-the-mathematical-library-of-the-future-20201001/ |archive-date= 2026-03-29|website=[[Quanta Magazine]]|date=October 2020 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Lean community |url=https://leanprover-community.github.io/lean3/ |access-date=2023-10-24 |website=leanprover-community.github.io}}</ref> As of May 2025, mathlib had formalized over 210,000 theorems and 100,000 definitions in Lean.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mathlib statistics |url=https://leanprover-community.github.io/mathlib_stats.html |access-date=2025-05-07 |website=leanprover-community.github.io}}</ref>

Other libraries include ''CSLib'' which is a theoretical computer science library,<ref>{{Cite web |title=CSLib |url=https://github.com/leanprover/cslib |access-date=2026-03-02 |website=[[GitHub]]}}</ref> ''SciLean'' which is a library for scientific computing in Lean,<ref>{{Cite web |title=SciLean |url=https://github.com/lecopivo/SciLean |access-date=2025-09-25 |website=[[GitHub]]}}</ref> and ''PhysLib'', whose goal is to digitize physics using Lean.<ref>{{Cite web |title=leanprover-community/physlib: A project to digitalise results from physics into Lean. |url=https://github.com/leanprover-community/physlib |access-date=2026-03-02 |website=[[GitHub]]}}</ref>

=== Editor integration ===

Lean integrates with
{{enum
| [[Visual Studio Code]]
| [[Neovim]]
| [[Emacs]]
}}.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Installing Lean 4 on Linux |url=https://leanprover-community.github.io/install/linux.html |access-date=2023-10-24 |website=leanprover-community.github.io}}</ref>
Interfacing is done via a client-extension and [[Language Server Protocol]] server. In these editors, [[Unicode]] symbols can be typed using [[LaTeX]]-like sequences, such as {{code|\times}} for "×".

==Examples (Lean 4)==

The [[natural numbers]] can be defined as an [[inductive type]]. This definition is based on the [[Peano axioms]] and states that every natural number is either zero or the [[Successor function|successor]] of some other natural number.
<syntaxhighlight lang="lean4">
inductive Nat : Type
  | zero : Nat
  | succ : Nat → Nat
</syntaxhighlight>

Addition of natural numbers can be [[Recursive definition|defined recursively]], using [[pattern matching]]. 
<syntaxhighlight lang="lean4">
def Nat.add : Nat → Nat → Nat
  | n, Nat.zero   => n                      -- n + 0 = n  
  | n, Nat.succ m => Nat.succ (Nat.add n m) -- n + succ(m) = succ(n + m)
</syntaxhighlight>

This is a simple proof of <math>(P \wedge Q) \implies (Q \wedge P)</math> for two [[proposition]]s {{mvar|P}} and {{mvar|Q}} (where {{and}} is the [[Logical conjunction|conjunction]] and <math>\implies</math> the [[Material conditional|implication]]) in Lean using tactic mode:
<syntaxhighlight lang="lean4">
theorem and_swap (p q : Prop) : p ∧ q → q ∧ p := by
  intro h            -- assume p ∧ q with proof h, the goal is q ∧ p
  apply And.intro    -- the goal is split into two subgoals, one is q and the other is p
  · exact h.right    -- the first subgoal is exactly the right part of h : p ∧ q
  · exact h.left     -- the second subgoal is exactly the left part of h : p ∧ q
</syntaxhighlight>

This same proof in term mode:
<syntaxhighlight lang="lean4">
theorem and_swap (p q : Prop) : p ∧ q → q ∧ p :=
  fun ⟨hp, hq⟩ => ⟨hq, hp⟩
</syntaxhighlight>

The theorem can also be proved using the grind tactic, which uses techniques from SMT solvers to automatically construct proofs:
<syntaxhighlight lang="lean4">
theorem and_swap (p q : Prop) : p ∧ q → q ∧ p := by
  grind
</syntaxhighlight>

== Usage ==

=== Mathematics ===

Lean has received attention from mathematicians such as [[Thomas Callister Hales|Thomas Hales]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Hales |first=Thomas |date=September 18, 2018 |title=A Review of the Lean Theorem Prover |url=https://jiggerwit.wordpress.com/2018/09/18/a-review-of-the-lean-theorem-prover/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20201121125544/https://jiggerwit.wordpress.com/2018/09/18/a-review-of-the-lean-theorem-prover/ |archive-date=21 Nov 2020 |website=Jigger Wit}}</ref> [[Kevin Buzzard]],<ref name="Buzzard" /> [[Terence Tao]],<ref>{{Cite web |last=Tao |first=Terence |date=31 May 2025 |title=A Lean companion to "Analysis I" |url=https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2025/05/31/a-lean-companion-to-analysis-i/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20250531182220/https://terrytao.wordpress.com/2025/05/31/a-lean-companion-to-analysis-i/ |archive-date=31 May 2025 |website=Terry Tao -- What's New |publisher=WordPress}}</ref> and Heather Macbeth.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Macbeth |first=Heather |title=The Mechanics of Proof |url=https://hrmacbeth.github.io/math2001/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240605090236/https://hrmacbeth.github.io/math2001/ |archive-date=5 Jun 2024 |website=hrmacbeth.github.io}}</ref> Hales is using it for his project, Formal Abstracts.<ref>{{cite web |title=Formal Abstracts |url=https://formalabstracts.github.io/ |website=Github}}</ref> Buzzard uses it for the Xena project.<ref>{{cite web |title=What is the Xena project? |url=https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/what-is-the-xena-project/ |website=Xena |language=en |date=8 May 2019}}</ref> One of the Xena Project's goals is to rewrite every theorem and proof in the undergraduate maths curriculum of [[Imperial College London]] in Lean. Tao released a Lean companion to his [[Real Analysis|real analysis]] textbook ''Analysis I'', consisting of a formalization of selected sections of the mathematical text.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Tao |first=Terence |title=analysis |url=https://github.com/teorth/analysis |website=github.com/teorth}}</ref> Macbeth is using Lean to teach students the fundamentals of mathematical proof with instant feedback.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Roberts |first=Siobhan |date=July 2, 2023 |title=A.I. Is Coming for Mathematics, Too |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2023/07/02/science/ai-mathematics-machine-learning.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240501080422/https://www.nytimes.com/2023/07/02/science/ai-mathematics-machine-learning.html |archive-date=1 May 2024 |website=New York Times}}</ref>

==== Noteworthy formalizations ====
{{See also|Proof assistant#Notable formalized proofs}}

In 2021, a team of researchers used Lean to verify the correctness of a proof by [[Peter Scholze]] in the area of [[condensed mathematics]]. The project garnered attention for formalizing a result at the cutting edge of mathematical research.<ref name="Quanta21">{{cite news |last=Hartnett |first=Kevin |date=July 28, 2021 |title=Proof Assistant Makes Jump to Big-League Math |work=[[Quanta Magazine]] |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/lean-computer-program-confirms-peter-scholze-proof-20210728/ |archive-url=https://archive.today/20220102145317/https://www.quantamagazine.org/lean-computer-program-confirms-peter-scholze-proof-20210728/ |archive-date=2 Jan 2022}}</ref> In 2023, Terence Tao used Lean to formalize a proof of the [[Freiman's theorem|Polynomial Freiman-Ruzsa]] (PFR) conjecture, a result published by Tao and collaborators in the same year.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sloman |first=Leila |date=2023-12-06 |title='A-Team' of Math Proves a Critical Link Between Addition and Sets |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/a-team-of-math-proves-a-critical-link-between-addition-and-sets-20231206/ |access-date=2023-12-07 |website=Quanta Magazine |language=en}}</ref> In 2026, [[List of conjectures by Paul Erdős|Erdős Problems]] 728,<ref>{{Cite web |title=728 |url=https://www.erdosproblems.com/728 |access-date=June 15, 2026 |website=Erdos Problems}}</ref> 347,<ref>{{Cite web |title=347 |url=https://www.erdosproblems.com/347 |access-date=June 15, 2026 |website=Erdos Problems}}</ref> and 369<ref>{{Cite web |title=369 |url=https://www.erdosproblems.com/369 |access-date=June 15, 2026 |website=Erdos Problems}}</ref> were solved using AI assistance and formally verified with Lean. 

=== Physics ===

Physlib<ref>{{cite web |title=Physlib |url=https://physlib.io}}</ref> aspires to be the definitive library for physics in Lean, akin to Mathlib for mathematics. It aims to be a comprehensive repository containing fundamental definitions, theorems, and calculations from physics.
[[Kevin Buzzard]] at [[Imperial College London]] says<ref name="New_Scientist_2026_03_26"> {{Cite news |title=New Scientist |date=2026-03-26 |website=[[New Scientist]] |url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/2520546-computer-finds-flaw-in-major-physics-paper-for-first-time |access-date=2026-04-12}}</ref> that formalization is having a big impact on mathematics, and that there is no reason that theoretical physics can not be treated in the same way. 
<blockquote>
“Ideally, we need a million lines of physics, and that might be hard work to get. If the machines aren’t pretty good at doing physics initially, then there’ll be manual work at the beginning, and then eventually the machines will hopefully take over”
</blockquote>

==== Noteworthy formalizations ====

In 2025, Joseph Tooby-Smith used Lean to discover an error<ref name="New_Scientist_2026_03_26"/> 
in a paper<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Maniatis |first1=M. |last2=von Manteuffel |first2=A. |last3=Nachtmann |first3=O. |last4=Nagel |first4=F. |title=Stability and symmetry breaking in the general two-Higgs-doublet model |journal=The European Physical Journal C |date=2006 |volume=48 |issue=3 |pages=805–823 |doi=10.1140/epjc/s10052-006-0016-6 |arxiv=hep-ph/0605184 |bibcode=2006EPJC...48..805M }} </ref> published in 2006 on the stability of the [[Two-Higgs-doublet model]] (2HDM) potential.

=== Artificial intelligence ===
{{See also|List of mathematical discoveries by artificial intelligence}}

In 2022, [[OpenAI]] and [[Meta AI]] independently created AI models to generate proofs of various high-school-level olympiad problems in Lean.<ref>{{Cite web |date=February 2, 2022 |title=Solving (some) formal math olympiad problems |url=https://openai.com/research/formal-math |access-date=March 13, 2024 |website=[[OpenAI]]}}</ref> Meta AI's model is available for public use with the Lean environment.<ref>{{Cite web |date=November 3, 2022 |title=Teaching AI advanced mathematical reasoning |url=https://ai.meta.com/blog/ai-math-theorem-proving/ |access-date=March 13, 2024 |website=[[Meta AI]]}}</ref>

In 2023, [[Vlad Tenev]] and Tudor Achim co-founded startup Harmonic, which aims to reduce [[Hallucination (artificial intelligence)|AI hallucinations]] by generating and checking Lean code.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Metz |first=Cade |date=23 September 2024 |title=Is Math the Path to Chatbots That Don't Make Stuff Up? |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/09/23/technology/ai-chatbots-chatgpt-math.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240924084639/https://www.nytimes.com/2024/09/23/technology/ai-chatbots-chatgpt-math.html |archive-date=24 Sep 2024 |work=New York Times}}</ref>

In 2024, [[Google DeepMind]] created [[Google DeepMind#AlphaProof|AlphaProof]]<ref>{{Cite web |date=2024-05-14 |title=AI achieves silver-medal standard solving International Mathematical Olympiad problems |url=https://deepmind.google/discover/blog/ai-solves-imo-problems-at-silver-medal-level/ |access-date=2024-07-25 |website=Google DeepMind |language=en}}</ref> which proves mathematical statements in Lean at the level of a silver medalist at the [[International Mathematical Olympiad]]. This was the first AI system that achieved a medal-worthy performance on a math olympiad's problems.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Roberts |first=Siobhan |date=July 25, 2024 |title=Move Over, Mathematicians, Here Comes AlphaProof |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2024/07/25/science/ai-math-alphaproof-deepmind.html |archive-url=https://archive.today/20240729121148/https://www.nytimes.com/2024/07/25/science/ai-math-alphaproof-deepmind.html |archive-date=July 29, 2024 |website=[[New York Times]]}}</ref>

In April 2025, [[DeepSeek]] introduced DeepSeek-Prover-V2, an AI model designed for theorem proving in Lean 4, built on top of DeepSeek-V3.<ref>{{cite web| url=https://au.finance.yahoo.com/news/deepseek-upgrades-math-focused-ai-122024021.html |title=DeepSeek upgrades its math-focused AI model Prover |date=April 30, 2025 |work=[[Yahoo Finance]] |accessdate=April 30, 2025}}</ref>

In 2026, AIs designed to spot bugs in software were directed at Lean, and found several loopholes which were then fixed.  Perhaps related to this effort, a purported disproof of the [[Collatz conjecture]] was announced as verified in Lean.  However, this proof was soon determined to rely on a bug in Lean, and once the bug was fixed the proof was found invalid.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://lawrencecpaulson.github.io/2026/07/30/Collatz.html |title=Why is it all in the kernel?}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Postmortem for Kernel Soundness Bug #14576 |url=https://leodemoura.github.io/blog/2026-8-1-postmortem-for-kernel-soundness-bug-14576/}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RnfFC_LowtU |title=The Collatz Conjecture was FALSE (for 2.5 days in July) |website=[[YouTube]] |date=30 July 2026 }}</ref>

In September 2026, [[Anthropic]] reported that agents running an internal research model comparable to [[Claude (AI)|Claude]] Fable 5.1 had produced a complete, machine-checked formalization of [[Fermat's Last Theorem]] in Lean 4 in eleven days.<ref name="anthropic-flt">{{cite web |title=Formalizing Fermat's Last Theorem |url=https://www.anthropic.com/research/formalizing-fermats-last-theorem |publisher=Anthropic |date=September 4, 2026 |access-date=September 8, 2026}}</ref><ref name="tnw-flt">{{cite news |last=Constantin |first=Ana Maria |title=Claude formalised Fermat's Last Theorem in 11 days |url=https://thenextweb.com/news/anthropic-claude-fermat-last-theorem-lean-buzzard |work=[[The Next Web]] |date=September 6, 2026 |access-date=September 8, 2026}}</ref> The proof followed the 1995 exposition by Darmon, Diamond and Taylor of [[Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem|Wiles's proof]], comprised about 13 million lines of Lean code and roughly 30,000 intermediate theorems, and relied only on Lean's three standard axioms; the agents coordinated through Prove2Me, a platform for collaborative formalization developed by Anthropic researcher Tianyi Peng and collaborators at [[Columbia University]].<ref name="anthropic-flt" /><ref>{{cite arXiv |last1=Chen |first1=S. |display-authors=etal |title=Prove2Me |year=2026 |class=cs.AI |eprint=2608.28433}}</ref> [[Kevin Buzzard]], who leads a separate [[Imperial College London]] project to formalize the theorem in Lean, compiled and checked the code and confirmed the result, while noting that it "adds nothing" mathematically to Wiles's proof and that the code could not be merged into Mathlib.<ref name="tnw-flt" /><ref name="buzzard-flt">{{cite web |last=Buzzard |first=Kevin |title=FLT: Anthropic has beaten me to it |url=https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/09/04/flt-anthropic-has-beaten-me-to-it/ |website=Xena Project |date=September 4, 2026 |access-date=September 8, 2026}}</ref> Buzzard said the Imperial project would continue.<ref name="buzzard-flt" />
